name: Crossings of a level, for any type
brief:
A signal counts how often a series crosses a level. The series may be prices in pence (`int`), sizes (`long long`) or prices as `double`, so write one function template `count_crossings(xs, level)`. Declare it with `template <typename T>`, returning `int`, with parameters `const std::vector<T>& xs` and `T level`.

A crossing is a move from strictly below the level to strictly above it, or back. A value equal to the level keeps the side the series was last on, and values at the level before any side is known are ignored.

For `{98, 101, 100, 99, 102}` and level 100 the series goes below, above, stays above at 100, then below and above again. The answer is 3.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 10^5$ values. The tests call the template with `int`, `long long`, `double` and a small struct that has only `<`.
`T` needs only `<`: use no other operator on it.
hint: Keep the last known side, -1 or +1, starting at 0 for not known. A value at the level changes nothing.
starter:
#include <vector>

// write the function template count_crossings(xs, level) here

examples.note: Below, above, still above at 100, below, above: three crossings.
The values at 100 before 101 belong to no side, so only 101 to 99 counts.

how: Submit runs 12 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The tests call it with `int`, `long long` and `double` vectors, and with a type that has only `<`.
notes: One template serves every type the tests use; the compiler writes a version for each `T`.
`level` has type `T` too, so a call passes a level of the same type as the vector's values.
Comparing only neighbours misses a crossing that pauses at the level, as 101, 100, 99 does.

planted.slip: Written for double only, so a vector of int or long long does not match.
Compares neighbours only, so a crossing that stops at the level on the way is missed.
Treats a value at the level as below it.

postlude:
struct Px { int p; };
bool operator<(Px a, Px b) { return a.p < b.p; }
